title: Early Voting Surges in 2026 Midterms: Democrats Hold Initial Edge, but Hispanic Turnout Steals the Spotlight
snippet: As nearly 33 million Americans cast early ballots ahead of the 2026 midterms, Democrats hold an early turnout advantage, though an unprecedented spike in Hispanic participation could redefine key battlegrounds.
content:
With Election Day just a week away, tens of millions of Americans have already cast their ballots in the 2026 midterm elections, offering political analysts an intriguing initial glimpse into voter behavior across the country. According to data tracked by the University of Florida’s Election Lab, nearly 33 million people have voted through early mail-in ballots and in-person voting windows—representing over a quarter of total turnout in the 2022 midterms.

Democrats Take Early Advantage, but GOP Catch-Up Looms

In the 27 states that track formal party registration, registered Democrats currently hold a notable lead over Republicans in early ballot submission. Democratic voters account for approximately 45% of early ballots cast so far, compared to 31% for Republicans, with unaffiliated voters making up the remaining 24%.

Political experts caution that an early Democratic advantage is standard practice in recent election cycles and does not guarantee a victory. Republicans historically make up significant ground on Election Day itself, when a higher percentage of GOP voters prefer to cast their ballots in person.

“We expect the Democrats to build up a lead in the early vote, and Election Day tends to be a Republican day, so you can't just look at the early vote as it is now,” noted Michael McDonald, a political science professor at the University of Florida who leads the Election Lab.

However, recent polling indicates that Democratic voter enthusiasm remains noticeably higher than GOP engagement. A struggling national economy and frustration over foreign policy continue to weigh on President Donald Trump, whose national approval rating sits near a term-low of 32%. Analysts suggest that GOP enthusiasm has dampened as a result, leading some conservative voters to sit out early voting windows.

Surging Hispanic Turnout Emerges as Key National Trend

While partisan splits draw heavy attention, strategists point to a dramatic surge in Hispanic voter participation as the defining trend of the early voting period. Early turnout among Hispanic voters is currently outpacing levels recorded at the same point during both the 2022 midterms and the 2024 presidential election.

The shift is especially prominent in sunbelt states like Texas, where a high-stakes Senate matchup between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton has drawn national spotlight. Hispanic voters represent 24% of early ballots cast in Texas so far, exceeding their total electorate share from the 2024 election cycle.

“If Hispanics are showing up in force now, it's almost with certainty going to change the overall diversity of the electorate in this election cycle,” McDonald said, adding that diverse states could see stronger-than-expected swings toward Democratic candidates.

Recent polling suggests widespread disapproval among Hispanic voters regarding economic pressures and immigration policy enforcement, reversing some of the gains the GOP made with the demographic in 2024.

What Early Data Really Means for Election Night

While political scientists remain traditionally cautious about using early turnout numbers to predict final winners, post-pandemic voting patterns have stabilized enough to offer meaningful indicators of overall electorate momentum.

With independent voters leaning heavily toward Democratic house candidates in recent national polls, campaigns on both sides are monitoring county-level early voting data intensely. Whether Republicans can mobilize a massive Election Day wave to offset Democratic early leads will decide control of Congress next week.
